To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CEA is an appropriate tool for comparing alternative ways of providing the same medical care to the same population, but it is not appropriate for comparing alternative medical care interventions.

CEA can be used to compare different interventions to treat the same medical condition but cannot be used to compare alternative interventions to treat different medical conditions or different diseases.

the use of C.E.A. in priority setting for health is appropriate only when the interventions compared are discrete alternatives, that the use of the cost per life-year gained to rank interventions is only justified under the restrictive assumption that the interventions compared are finite and discrete, and that the use of cost-effectiveness analysis to inform resource allocation among different health interventions is only appropriate under the unrealistic assumption that the interventions are finite alternatives that cannot be scaled up or down.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CEA should not be used as the sole tool for setting priorities among different interventions for the fight against HIV.
CEA can be used to compare alternatives to treat the same medical condition and to inform resource allocation among programmes to fight the epidemic.
CEA is not a good tool for setting priorities among different health programmes for the fight against HIV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cost-effectiveness algorithm is an important tool for decision-making but it is not the only one and should be used in conjunction with other tools.
the use of CEs to inform resource allocation decisions in the fight against AIDS is not a panacea.
, in the fight against AIDS, CEA should be considered as one of many criteria to be used in priority setting, not as a substitute for political and ethical decisions about resource allocation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cost-effectiveness analysis is not a panacea for setting priorities among different interventions to combat HIV/AIDS, but rather a tool that should be used with caution and in conjunction with other methods of analysis.
the use of cost-effectiveness analysis to inform priority setting in public policy is not straightforward, and requires a pragmatic and flexible interpretation of the results of this economic tool.
cost-effectiveness analyses are not the only way to make decisions about resource allocation.
